info.name: IFF Dataspace — Data Push & Pull
info.description:
Pure data **push and pull** against the IFF Dataspace gateway — send as a factory
owner, receive as a machine builder. Governance endpoints (capability requests/policy,
conversation state) are deliberately left out; this is the transfer path only.

### Setup

1. Fill in `gatewayUrl`, `keycloakUrl`, `realm`.
2. Fill in `foParticipantId`/`foClientSecret` and `mbParticipantId`/`mbClientSecret` — the
   Keycloak `client_id` **is** the participant URN. Get the secrets from the management GUI
   (Participants → Show credentials) or, with an admin token,
   `GET {managementUrl}/api/participants/{participant_id}/credentials`.
   Treat them as secrets: use a Postman environment or vault variables rather than committing
   real values back into this file.
3. Run **0 · Tokens** — the test scripts store `foToken` / `mbToken`, which every other request
   uses. Tokens live ~5 minutes; a 401 later just means re-run them.
4. Run **1 · Push** as FO, then **2 · Pull** as MB. `messageId` is threaded automatically from
   send to receive.

### How the two sides connect

```
FO app ──POST /outbox/messages──▶ gateway ──▶ FO adapter ···EDC data plane···▶ MB adapter ◀──GET /inbox/messages── MB app
```

The gateway reads `participant_id` from the JWT and proxies to *that* participant's own
adapter — the token alone decides which side you are acting as, and there is no way to reach
another participant's adapter. Payload bytes never travel through the gateway: the receiver's
connector pulls them directly over the EDC data plane. `/internal/*` paths are blocked (404).

Sending is asynchronous (202 + background EDC workflow) and receiving is **polling** — no
push/webhook/SSE transport exists today. The two "poll until…" requests self-retry in the
Collection Runner (max 15 attempts); set the Runner's Delay to ~2000 ms.

### Errors

| HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 401 | missing/expired JWT — re-run the token request |
| 403 | no `participant_id` claim, participant not in the registry, or same-type send |
| 404 | `internal/` path (blocked), or the message doesn't exist yet on the receiving side |
| 409 | conversation state violation (e.g. already closed) |
| 422 | structural violation (wrong required/forbidden fields for the performative) |
| 503 / 504 | gateway cannot reach, or timed out waiting on, the adapter |

A duplicate or race-losing `close` is not an error: 202 with `"applied": false`.

### Source of truth

IFF-Dataspace: `gateway-api.md` (full reference), `flow.md` (end-to-end walkthrough),
`asyncapi.yaml` (per-performative message schemas). A self-hosted (external) participant uses
these exact paths against its own adapter directly, with no gateway in the path.

item.name: 0 · Tokens & discovery
item.description:
Run both token requests first. Everything below inherits the token through the
`foToken` / `mbToken` variables — the gateway reads `participant_id` from the JWT
and proxies to *that* participant's own adapter, so the token alone decides which
side you are acting as. There is no way to reach another participant's adapter.

request.description:
Mint the factory owner participant token via Keycloak `client_credentials`.

`client_id` **is** the participant URN — the Keycloak client is created when the
participant is registered. Get the secret from the management GUI
(Participants → Show credentials) or
`GET {managementUrl}/api/participants/{id}/credentials` with an admin token.

Saves `access_token` into the `foToken` collection variable. Tokens are short-lived
(~5 min) — any later 401 means re-run this request.

exec: try { body = pm.response.json(); } catch (e) { body = null; }
console.warn('no access_token in the response — foToken left unchanged');

request.description:
Registered participants of the *opposite* type — what this token holder may
send to. Cross-type rule: FO→FO or MB→MB sends are rejected with 403.

Populates `mbParticipantId` from the first result if that variable is still empty.

item.name: 1 · Push — as Factory Owner
item.description:
The send side. `POST /outbox/messages` returns **202 immediately** with a
`message_id`; the EDC negotiation and transfer then run in the background, so poll
`/status` to confirm the message actually left.

Three content modes, same endpoint family:

| Mode | What the adapter does |
|---|---|
| `payload` (inline JSON) | uploads it to the sender's own MinIO, registers an ad-hoc EDC asset, keeps only a `payload_ref` |
| `content_ref` | nothing — relays `{asset_id, dsp_url}` as-is; the bytes never touch this adapter |
| `POST /outbox/files` | bundles the uploaded files into one ZIP and transfers that |

Supplying both `payload` and `content_ref` on one message is rejected as ambiguous (422).

The payload is never persisted next to the protocol fields — inline `payload` is a
caller convenience, not the storage model.

request.description:
The ordinary data push. Saves `message_id` into `messageId` for the pull folder.

**Fields**

| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `receiver_participant` | yes | must be the opposite participant type, else 403 |
| `payload` | — | any JSON object; delivered verbatim |
| `performative` | no (`inform`) | `request`, `inform`, `grant`, `deny`, `cancel`, `close`, `reopen`, `escalate`, `deescalate` |
| `capability` | depends | FO offers `twin:direct` (auto), `twin:adjacents`, `twin:history` (both on-request); MB offers `mb:confidential` |
| `conversation_id` | no | generated if omitted; reuse it to keep a thread together |
| `reply_expected` | no (`false`) | hint to the receiver |

**Responses** — 202 `{message_id, status:"pending", applied, conversation_state}`.
422 if the performative's required/forbidden fields are wrong; 409 if the
conversation is already closed (neither ever reaches EDC).

Note the capability policy layer is **not** enforced on this path — a `denied`
policy does not block the send. Check `GET /capabilities/access?provider=…`
yourself before sending if that matters to your app.

Bring-your-own-asset push: the content already exists on a connector you
control, and you hand over only a pointer. No upload happens and no local EDC
asset is created — the reference is relayed as-is, and the receiver negotiates
for it over standard DSP exactly as for any other message.

`asset_id` defaults here to `asset-{{messageId}}` — the deterministic id the
adapter assigns to an inline send — so this request works right after the
previous one without standing up a second connector. Set
`ownConnectorDspUrl` to the connector that actually holds the asset
(`http://connector-<slug>.dataspace-participants.svc.cluster.local:8082/api/v1/dsp`
for a hosted participant, or your own connector's DSP endpoint if self-hosted).

The sender's own record afterwards shows `content_ref` set and `payload_ref: null`.

formdata.description: Pick one or more local files — attach as many as you like under this same key.

request.description:
`multipart/form-data` push. The adapter bundles every attached file into a
single ZIP, transfers that over EDC, and the receiver downloads one archive
regardless of how many files you sent.

**Select files in the `files` row before sending** — Postman cannot store file
paths in an exported collection, so the row arrives empty and the request
fails validation until you pick something.

`performative` (default `inform`), `capability` and `conversation_id` behave
exactly as on `POST /outbox/messages` — a file bundle is a normal message whose
content happens to be a ZIP, not a separate performative. The resulting inbox
entry has `has_files: true`.

Sender-side lifecycle:

```
pending → registered → notified
                    ↘ error
rejected   (terminal — state-machine violation, never reached EDC)
```

`notified` is the **terminal success state for the sender** — the receiver's
connector pulls independently, so there is deliberately no "delivered" state
here. Confirm actual arrival from the receiving side instead.

The test script re-runs this request until `notified` (max 15 attempts) when
executed in the Collection Runner. Set the Runner's per-request **Delay to
~2000 ms** so it doesn't hammer the gateway; a single manual Send just reports
the current status once.

exec: // Postman renamed setNextRequest; support both runtimes.
try { body = pm.response.json(); } catch (e) { body = null; }
console.log('sender side complete: notified — receiver is pulling over the EDC data plane');
console.warn('terminal failure: ' + status + ' — ' + (body.error_message || 'see the record for details'));
console.warn('gave up after ' + MAX_POLLS + ' polls; last status: ' + status);
setNext(pm.info.requestName);   // re-runs this request; Collection Runner only

request.description:
Full sender-side record: protocol fields plus `payload_ref` / `content_ref` and
the EDC ids. Useful to prove the content/protocol split actually happened —
an inline send shows `payload_ref: "minio://…"` with `content_ref: null`, never
the payload itself.

item.name: 2 · Pull — as Machine Builder
item.description:
The receive side, and it is **polling** — there is no push, webhook or SSE transport
today (`asyncapi.yaml` models the same message shapes so one could be added later
without changing them).

What crosses the protocol layer is only a notification (`message_id`, `asset_id`,
`provider_dsp_url`, protocol fields) — never the payload. The receiving adapter
stores that row immediately (`status: negotiating`), then separately tells its *own*
EDC connector to pull the bytes into its *own* MinIO (`status: received`). The
`payload` you read below is composed from those two halves at read time.

Two things that bite pollers:

- `?status=received` **excludes** messages still `negotiating`, so one empty result
  does not mean nothing is in flight — keep polling on a schedule.
- After ack, the content is purged at `CONTENT_RETENTION_HOURS` (default 1 day) while
  the metadata row survives `CONTROL_PLANE_RETENTION_HOURS` (default 30 days) — so an
  old acked message reads back with an empty `payload` and `has_files: false`. Read
  the content before you ack it.

request.description:
Newest first. Drop the `status` query param to see everything including
`negotiating` (in flight), `acked` and `error`.

Each entry carries `payload`, `performative`, `capability`, `conversation_id`,
`sender_participant` and `has_files` — this is the whole worker-loop input:
list → handle → ack.

Fetch one message by id — `messageId` is set by the push folder, or set it
yourself to pull something a counterpart sent independently.

Expect **404 for the first second or two**: the row only exists once the
sender's notification lands. Then `negotiating` → `received` as this side's own
EDC pull completes. `payload` is populated once `received`.

Self-retries up to 15 times in the Collection Runner (set the Runner Delay to
~2000 ms); a single manual Send reports the current state once.

exec: // Postman renamed setNextRequest; support both runtimes.
try { body = pm.response.json(); } catch (e) { body = null; }
console.warn('terminal failure: ' + status + ' — ' + (body.error_message || 'see the record for details'));
console.warn('gave up after ' + MAX_POLLS + ' polls; last status: ' + status);
setNext(pm.info.requestName);   // re-runs this request; Collection Runner only

request.description:
Streams the ZIP for a message where `has_files` is true — 400 otherwise.
Comes back as `application/octet-stream` with
`Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="<message_id>.zip"`.

Use Postman's **Send and Download** (the arrow next to Send) to write it to
disk; a plain Send renders the bytes in the response pane instead.

Marks the message processed (`status` → `acked`). Returns **204 No Content** and
is idempotent.

This starts the content-retention clock: the MinIO object is purged after
`CONTENT_RETENTION_HOURS` (default 1 day, or the sender's `expires_at` if set),
after which `payload` reads empty and `has_files` reads false. Read and store
what you need **before** acking.
